segments.text: 4,900 hectares of Hacienda, Louis Sita stayed under owner control through shares, not titles. This is unintended consequences, episode 148. The path runs from why lawmakers offered a corporate shortcut through the vote that enrolled the estate to the gap between paper ownership and the person who signs a land use permit. Then to what the courts later ordered, and finally to attest anyone writing an ownership rule can run before the ink is dry. The law grew out of decades of rural unrest.
Repeated attempts at land reform had left tenancy rates high.
Families who tilled large estates still did not hold them.
In June of 1988, Congress passed the comprehensive agrarian reform law to transfer those estates
to the families who worked them.
President Corazon Aquino signed Republic Act 6657 on 10 June 1988.
Her own family owned Hacienda, Louisita in Tarlac.
The 1986 People Power Revolt had raised expectations that concentrated land holdings would finally
be broken up.
Signing a redistribution statute, with that family name attached to one of the estates
in view, was the political answer to those expectations.
Lawmakers still had a practical fear.
They believed compulsory subdivision of integrated plantations would disrupt production.
New owners they argued might be left without credit or equipment.
Many estates already ran as integrated sugar or rice operations, with shared irrigation
and shared milling.
Breaking those links risk lowering output at a moment when the post-Marcos economy needed
steady agricultural exports.
So Section 31 offered another route.
A corporate plantation could stay intact.
Workers would receive minority shares and a production bonus instead of title to particular
fields.
The Department of Agrarian Reform, and the Presidential Agrarian Reform Council, treated
that option as one legitimate path to the law's stated goal of land to the tiller.
The arithmetic they worked with was straightforward.
A single large corporation could issue shares representing the land's value.
Those shares could be spread across thousands of workers over 30 years.
The corporation could still meet production targets that small plots might not sustain.
by allowing the stock route, the framers hoped to avoid political backlash from landowners.
They also hoped to avoid the administrative burden of surveying and titling every
hectare at once. Read on its own terms, the clause was a compromise between speed,
efficiency, and a promise of ownership. It assumed that a share in the company that held
the land was close enough to a share of the land itself. Hacienda Luisita
Incorporated Submitted Its Stock Distribution Plan in 1989.
A referendum that year recorded 92.9% approval among Farm Worker Beneficiaries, according
to Department of Agrarian Reform Records.
That figure, as the Department recorded it, became the Democratic warrant for the plan.
Workers received 33.296% of the shares, distributed over 30 years, plus a 3% production share.
The share percentage was calculated from the ratio of the land's declared value
to the corporation's total equity. Farm workers technically owned a slice of the company
rather than individual parcels. The remaining equity stayed with the original shareholders.
The co-huanko family therefore continued to elect the board and to set land use policy.
The 3% production share was an annual cash distribution tied to gross sales. It was meant
to give workers immediate income while the stock vested. The Presidential Agrarian Reform
Council approved the plan. Similar arrangements were later adopted on other corporate estates.
Government reports at the time highlighted the rapid enrollment of large holdings under
the new mechanism. Early tallies counted these plans as successful coverage under the law.
The paperwork showed workers listed as beneficiaries on corporate books. From the agency side,
that listing looked like progress. A vast estate had entered the program without a survey crew walking
every boundary, and without splitting mills and canals into fragments. From the family side,
the corporation remained one decision-maker. Majority voting control never left the original owners.
Skeptics of physical breakup had a clean reply in those early years. Production links stayed whole,
and workers had both a vesting schedule and a cash bonus tied to sales. What the enrollment numbers
could not show was who would sign the next permit, because the stock plan left the co-huanko
family with majority voting control, day-to-day management stayed with the original owners,
so did land use decisions. The causal chain ran through the voting arithmetic,
with only about one-third of the shares, workers could never outvote the family on whether to sell
or rezone land. When the corporation later sought conversion permits for non-agricultural use,
The minority state gave workers no formal seat at the table.
Portions of the estate were reclassified for industrial parks and sold.
Additional hectares were taken for the Subic Clark-Tarlac Expressway.
That expressway alone removed several hundred hectares from agricultural production.
The compensation paid to the corporation flowed to the majority shareholders.
Philippine Institute for Development Studies, Researchers, Marifee Ballesteros, and colleagues
later documented how the same mechanism worked beyond this one estate.
Together with conversion permits and with registration of excess land to relatives,
it allowed several estates to avoid physical redistribution.
Farm workers who held minority shares received dividends that fluctuated with corporate performance.
They did not receive secure title they could mortgage or pass to errors.
Workers who had expected eventual land titles found themselves holding paper whose value depended on corporate profitability
reality, rather than on the rising price of farmland itself.
Over time, some families sold their vested shares for immediate cash.
Those sales concentrated ownership further back inside the original corporate structure.
A 2004 strike by the Alianza Nang Mang Mangagawang Bukit Nang Haseyenda Luisita brought renewed
attention to the gap between promised benefits and actual control.
The pattern was not a one-off failure of paperwork.
The law's alternative compliance path rewarded owners who maintained corporate form while the physical
land stayed under unified management. On other estates where stock plans were approved,
the same reward applied. Keep the company, issue the minority slice, count the workers as covered,
decide as the board what the land becomes. That is a second order effect of measuring success by
enrollment rather than by who holds the vote. A third order effect followed when land left
agriculture. Once parcels were converted, leased, or taken for a highway, the thing workers
might someday have titled was no longer the same estate they had been told they were
joining. Dividends could rise or fall with whatever the corporation earned after that
change. They could not restore a field that had already been re-zoned. The Presidential
Agrarian Reform Council's 2005 Revocation Order said the stock plan had not done what
the statute required. The Supreme Court's rulings in 2011 and 2012 confirmed that the plan had
not transferred effective ownership. Those decisions did not invent a new theory of control.
They read the voting arithmetic that had been visible since the shares were issued.
After the Supreme Court decisions, compulsory acquisition proceeded on the remaining agricultural land.
The last certificates of land ownership award for Hacienda, Louisita, were issued in 2018.
That distribution occurred under compulsory acquisition orders that valued the land as
of the 1989 taking date.
Compensation therefore reflected earlier prices rather than current market rates.
Even after the shares were set aside, some converted parcels had already been sold or
leased for industrial use.
The redistributed agricultural remainder was smaller than the original estate.
The Balistero study for the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that the overall
program had distributed roughly 4.7 million hectares by 2016, yet many large
estates remained intact through the very options the 1988 law had permitted. The
review noted that aggregate hectares distributed looks substantial. The
persistence of large contiguous holdings showed that evasion routes built into
the original statute had limited the program's structural impact. Subsequent
administrations tightened conversion rules. They removed the stock
distribution provision from later extensions of the program. The fix arrived after the alternative
path had already done its work on the ground. A revocation can unwind a plan that is still a plan.
It cannot unsell a parcel that has changed hands, or put back hectares already taken for a road.
When Congress wrote the stock distribution clause into the law, it rewarded landowners who could
keep corporate control while satisfying the letter of redistribution. Later regulators responded
by revoking plans that left voting power unchanged.
That sequence shows that an ownership rule has to be measured by who actually decides land use,
not by whose name appears on a beneficiary list.
The same pattern appears whenever a reform statute creates an alternative compliance path
without requiring a transfer of decision rights.
Coverage can look complete on a ledger while the board that signs the permit never changes.
A cash bonus tied to sales can arrive on time and still leave the land use vote where
it started.
If you are watching a present day housing, farm, or corporate governance bill that offers
shares, units, or paper stakes in place of the asset itself, the tell is simple.
Ask whether the new arrangement changes the identity of the person or the board that signs
the next permit.
If it does not, the statute has created a record of inclusion without moving control.
How might today's policy makers test whether a new ownership rule truly shifts control
before it is written into law?
